media.transcript: Welcome to Satan's Kingdom in Massachusetts, where today we're going to be answering the question you've probably had for about four seconds now. What's in that town? You can still see me, can't you? For starters, Satan's Kingdom isn't a town. It's a part of Northfield, Massachusetts on the Vermont border. It's an old name for the northwest part of Northfield, across the Connecticut River from downtown. Historically, it refers to that whole section of town, but these days it mostly refers to the Satan's Kingdom Wildlife Management Area, which is open for hunting, fishing, and hiking. It does still appear on official town maps, just north of a landmark called Hell's Kitchen. Where did the name come from? According to local legend, the name stems from a man who had just left a church sermon that depicted the fires of Hell, saw a forest fire across the river, and said that Satan's kingdom was burning. These days you don't see the name much outside of curiosity on maps. The only places I found the name publicly posted were at the entrances to the Wildlife Management Area in Northfield and nearby Bernardston. So what's in and around Satan's kingdom? Not a lot. Lots of trees and some mysteries, like this pair of glasses that were jammed into a sign, this tree that fell across the trail, and these signs that have zero information on them. Outside the wildlife management area, I did find this old truck for sale and noticed that Pioneer Valley Regional School was just around the corner. I also took some time to explore that place called Hell's Kitchen, which it turns out is just a marshy little inlet with no devils, but definitely signs of beavers. I'm pretty sure I had to walk across a dam to get to it. There's nothing supernatural about the area, but it is important to be mindful of private property lines as well as active hunting in the area. The Satan's Kingdom area was once a hotspot for growing beer hops. That legacy continues in Northfield across the river at Four Star Farms, where they grow hops and put out some amazing beers at their brewery. It's the perfect spot to sit back and wonder, seriously, what was up with those glasses? What town should we visit next? Let us know in the comments. media.transcript: Here's how I would spend three days on your first trip to Mexico City. It feels like there's a million recommendations for Mexico City these days, which can make trip planning feel really overwhelming. So here's how I'd map out three days to hit some of the city's top spots. Is it a little touristy? Yes, but there's a reason these places are so popular, and this itinerary lets you see a lot of them in a short amount of time. Start your first day early with coffee and pastries. If you want to see what all the hype is about, definitely head to Panaderia Rosetta, but get there early because the line does get long. I do think it's worth it to try at least once. Their pastries are delicious in my opinion, and the famous guava roll lived up to the hype. But this is definitely not your only option. And there are so many incredible bakeries and cafes all over the city. Since you'll be in Roma Norte, you can just wander around for a bit. I think this is one of the prettiest neighborhoods. Walk through El Parian. This is the beautiful interiors you see here. There are little shops, another coffee shop. And then make your way to Jenny's Quesadillas. Let's call this your late morning snack or early lunch, but heads up, you do need cash here. Stroll through Parque Mexico, and then you'll be in the beautiful Condesa neighborhood with more. In the afternoon, take a short Uber ride up to Chapultepec Castle. Entry costs about $10, and I think it's absolutely worth it to walk around. The grounds are so beautiful. You can see inside and then a great overview of the entire city. After freshening up a bit, head to Mi Compachava or Contramar for dinner, and then Baltrobar after for drinks. Okay, for day two, you have two options. Option one is a full day trip to Grutas Tolantongo. We left the city at 4 a.m. and we got back at 4 p.m. So it's absolutely doable in one day. It is a very long day, but I thought it was completely worth it. We started in these beautiful hot springs, got a bit of breakfast, then headed over to this waterfall, swam around, then ended the day at the Natural River. It didn't feel crowded at the times we went, so I really recommend going with a tour who knows the best times to go. I would plan a more casual dinner that night, just grabbing tacos at a local spot. Your second option for day two is a shorter day trip that's just about 45 minutes outside of the city. I would still probably leave early in the morning, so you can try to miss the afternoon traffic on the way back. For this one, you'll start at the Frida Kahlo Museum, then wander through the Coyoacan Market, and then head to Sochimoco to spend the afternoon on one of the colorful boats, which are usually all you can drink and turn into a little party. I'd book a later dinner this day, somewhere like Martinez, Lardo, or Quintanillo. I've linked both these experiences in my bio if you want to see the exact ones I recommend. Start day three with a quick breakfast somewhere like Cafe Mila. and then drive 45 minutes out to Tiotiwakan. This is where you can do the famous hot air balloon ride, which if you're doing that, you're actually gonna start way earlier because they're usually at sunrise. Otherwise, you can just walk around the pyramids and learn a bit of the history. After that, drive just a few minutes over to have lunch at La Gruta.
